In the autumn of 1991, President George H.W. Bush announced unilateral withdrawals of American nuclear weapons. This briefing book, posted in September 2016, covers that pullback and the answer it drew from Moscow. The Soviet Union matched the move with rapid cuts of its own.

Unilateral means Washington did not wait for a treaty or a negotiation. It simply withdrew whole classes of weapons and invited a response. That gamble produced one of the fastest nuclear reductions of the Cold War, weeks before the Soviet Union itself dissolved. The documents show disarmament by announcement, a method arms control rarely attempts.

In 1957 the CIA debriefed a witness who had seen a Soviet hydrogen bomb test up close. William Burr edited this briefing book, number 623, published in April 2018. It presents newly declassified intelligence reports from 1957 on Soviet atomic development.

The witness described air crackling with pressure, as if the air was tearing up. CIA analysis also credited German scientists with greatly accelerating Soviet nuclear research. Eyewitness color of that kind is rare in intelligence files, which usually trade in estimates and photographs. The reports show analysts piecing together a rival's bomb program from human fragments in the years before satellites.

Greenland's size and position made it vital to American defense in the early Cold War, and nuclear plans followed. This briefing book is the first part of a series on episodes in that nuclear history, from 1947 to 1968. Its named landmark is Thule Air Base, the early-warning site in the far north.

Iceland sat astride the North Atlantic sea lanes, yet no American nuclear weapons were ever deployed there during the Cold War. The record matters because the debate happened at all: geography kept pulling planners toward a country whose consent was doubtful, and restraint, in the end, won.

govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_vietnam_:
South Vietnamese president Ngo Dinh Diem was overthrown and killed in a coup in November 1963, with American knowledge. Briefing Book number 730, edited by John Prados and Luke Nichter and published in November 2020, brings new evidence to that old event, including material from President John Kennedy's own files.

A newly released Kennedy tape and the president's intelligence checklists fill gaps in the known record. They suggest Kennedy leaned toward regime change more strongly than earlier accounts believed. Most striking are notes by Diem himself, published for the first time, written hours before his assassination. For readers, the release sharpens the hardest question of the Vietnam story's first act: how far did Washington go in toppling its own ally?

trithemius-steganographia-latin:
Abbot Johannes Trithemius wrote the Steganographia, a book of secret writing, around 1500. It circulated in manuscript and was printed in Latin in 1608. Trithemius was a famed scholar of codes and monastic learning.

On the surface, the book teaches how to call spirits for messages. Inside, its lists and tables hide a true cipher system. Scholars long debated which face was real. The work earned its author a dark name for magic. It remains a Renaissance crypto classic, read by code historians and occultists alike for its double game. Its double face still draws new readers today.
ficino-de-vita-libri-tres-1498-latin:
Marsilio Ficino, the leading thinker of Florence's Platonic Academy, wrote Three Books on Life in 1489. The Latin text here comes from the Venice edition of 1498. The work is a guide to health for scholars, built on astrology, medicine, and natural magic.

Ficino teaches readers how to guard their health, live long, and draw strength from the planets and stars. He covers diet, sleep, herbs, music, and talismans, the images meant to catch heavenly power. The book, with its added defense of his magic, became the base work of Renaissance medical astrology.
pico-oratio-de-hominis-dignitate-latin:
Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, a young Italian count and scholar, wrote his Oration on the Dignity of Man in 1486. He meant it as the opening speech for a public debate on 900 claims about philosophy and faith. The Latin text is the speech as he prepared it.

Pico argues that humans have no fixed place in creation and can shape themselves by free choice. He defends learning from many sources at once, including Jewish Kabbalah and learned magic. Later readers named the speech the manifesto of the Renaissance, and it still anchors debates on human freedom.
reuchlin-de-arte-cabalistica-1517-latin:
Johannes Reuchlin, a German lawyer and scholar of Hebrew, published De arte cabalistica at Hagenau in 1517. The Latin work, in three books, is the founding text of Christian Kabbalah. It mixes Hebrew and Greek passages into a staged debate among three speakers.

Simon the Kabbalist, Marranus the Muslim, and Philolaus the Pythagorean argue over the Messiah, number lore, and the hands-on use of Kabbalah. Reuchlin aimed to show that Jewish mystic teaching could support Christian truth. The book shaped how Europe's scholars read Kabbalah for the next two centuries.
dee-monas-hieroglyphica-latin:
John Dee, adviser and astrologer to Queen Elizabeth I, published his Monas Hieroglyphica at Antwerp in 1564. The Latin text here follows the Frankfurt edition of 1591. Dee built the whole book around one symbol, his Hieroglyphic Monad, a glyph he designed himself.

In 24 short theorems, Dee unpacks the glyph line by line. He reads into it math, astronomy, alchemy, and Kabbalah, claiming one sign holds the keys to nature. Scholars of magic and early science still mine the book, though much of its meaning stays locked in Dee's private code. Few Renaissance books are stranger or more studied.
rituale-romanum-latin:
The Rituale Romanum is the Catholic Church's official book of rites outside the Mass. Pope Paul V issued the first edition in 1614. The Latin text here is the standard 1925 edition from Ratisbon, which kept the older rites in their classic form.

Priests use the book for baptisms, weddings, funerals, blessings, and prayers for the sick and dying. Its most famous part is the Rite of Exorcism, word for word the same since 1614. The book shows the Church's daily ritual life as it stood before the reforms of the 1960s. Latinists value its exact, formal wording.
spee-cautio-criminalis-1631-latin:
Friedrich Spee was a German Jesuit priest who heard the last words of many women condemned as witches. His Cautio Criminalis, printed at Rinteln in 1631, attacks the witch trials from inside the system. The Latin text is that of the first edition.

Spee lays out 51 doubts about how the trials worked. He shows how torture forced false claims, how one claim led to the next arrest, and why no accused person could ever prove innocence. The book helped turn opinion in Germany against the burnings. It remains one of the bravest books of the witch-trial age.
delrio-disquisitiones-magicae-latin:
Martín Antonio Del Rio was a Flemish Jesuit scholar whose Disquisitiones Magicae first came out at Leuven in 1599 and 1600. The six Latin books form a vast storehouse of demon lore. Later writers on witchcraft leaned on it so hard that some call it a new Catholic Malleus.

Del Rio works through sabbaths, pacts, fortune-telling, astrology, raising the dead, and natural magic. He sorts true wonders from fraud and from the devil's tricks, citing hundreds of older writers. The set became the learned reference on magic and witch trials for more than a century.
sinistrari-demoniality-1879-english-lati:
Ludovico Maria Sinistrari was a Franciscan friar and demon expert in late 1600s Italy. His Latin treatise on demoniality stayed in manuscript until it was found in 1872. The first English version came out at Paris in 1879, printed side by side with the Latin.

Sinistrari argues that incubi and succubi, the night demons of old lore, are real bodily beings with minds of their own. He asks how the law and the Church should judge acts tied to them. The odd, careful book is a late high point of Catholic demon thought.
allan-quatermain:
H. Rider Haggard sent his hunter hero Allan Quatermain on his last trek in this book of 1887. It is the mate to King Solomon's Mines, the hit of two years past. Haggard wrote it while the fame of the first book was still fresh and high.

Quatermain, now old, joins a last hunt for a lost white race in the heart of Africa. Strange priests, a vast cave world, and a doom that hangs on the band fill the tale. The book turns the brisk hunter of the first tale into a figure of myth.
the-glittering-plain:
William Morris wrote this tale of a quest in a made up land in 1891. Its full name is The Story of the Glittering Plain. Morris, poet and craftsman, had by then made his own line of prose romance in a high, old style.

A young man of the Raven kindred sails to seek his lost bride in the Glittering Plain. That land grants long life, yet its gift turns sour for those who take it and stay. The book is a landmark of the fantasy line Morris made, the line that taught Tolkien his craft.
albumasar-introductorium-1489-latin:
Abu Ma'shar of Baghdad, called Albumasar in Latin, wrote the Great Introduction to astrology in the ninth century. It became the book that taught the Latin West the Arabic system of the art. Hermann of Dalmatia turned it into Latin, and the version here was printed in 1489. No English version in the public domain exists.

Albumasar grounds the power of the stars in physics, sorting signs, planets, houses, and aspects into one great scheme. Kings and scholars across Europe used his book to read the heavens for three centuries. The printed Latin of 1489 shows the work at the height of its fame. It stands as the record of how Arabic astrology remade a science in the West.
alcabitius-isagoge-1521-latin:
Al-Qabisi, a scholar of Aleppo in the tenth century, wrote the Isagoge as a short first book for students of astrology. For the rest of the Middle Ages it served as the standard beginner's text in the Latin West. The edition here is the Latin printing from Venice in 1521, with the commentary of John of Saxony.

Five chapters lay out the signs, the planets, the houses, and the terms a judge of the stars must know. John of Saxony, a Paris master of the 1300s, explains each point for the classroom. No English version in the public domain exists. The little book shows how a whole science was taught, one clear rule at a time.
ficino-pimander-1481-latin:
In 1463 Marsilio Ficino set aside his Plato to translate a Greek manuscript that had just reached Florence: the discourses of Hermes Trismegistus. His Latin version, the Pimander, was printed in 1481. It lit the Hermetic fever of the Renaissance. No English version of Ficino's own text exists in the public domain.

The discourses tell of God as light and life, the making of the world, and the fall and return of man. Ficino and his readers took Hermes for a sage older than Moses, a gentile prophet of Christian truth. The book reshaped Renaissance thought on magic, the soul, and the stars. This early printing is the form in which Europe first read it.
remy-daemonolatreiae-1595-latin:
Nicolas Rémy, a judge in Lorraine, published his Daemonolatreiae Libri Tres, Three Books on the Worship of Demons, at Lyon in 1595. The text is the Latin original. Rémy drew his book from the capital trials of some nine hundred persons put to death for witchcraft in his own courts. With the Malleus Maleficarum, it is the most weighty early work on demons and witches.

Case by case he tells of pacts, sabbaths, weather magic, and the marks of the devil, all sworn in his courtroom. Rémy believed every word and hanged on the strength of it. His casebook armed a generation of judges across Europe. The library holds the English version beside this Latin root of it.
eymerich-directorium-inquisitorum-1578-l:
Nicholas Eymerich, inquisitor of Aragon, wrote the Directorium Inquisitorum in 1376, the manual that taught inquisitors their trade for two hundred years. The text here is the Rome edition of 1578, with the commentaries of Francisco Peña. Eymerich wrote from a hard life of hunting heresy in Catalonia and at the papal court.

The manual covers the whole craft: how heresy is found, how witnesses are heard, how torture is ruled, and how sentences are framed. Its sections on witchcraft and sorcery later fed the Malleus tradition of the witch trials. Peña's notes bring the old text up to the age of the Spanish Inquisition. It is the procedural root of the early modern persecution.
erastus-repetitio-disputationis-lamiis-1:
Thomas Erastus, the Swiss Reformed doctor and theologian, wrote this Repetition of the Disputation on Witches at Basel in 1578. The Latin text answers Johann Weyer, the great skeptic who held that accused witches were melancholy women fooled by the devil, not partners with him. Their clash is the great sixteenth-century debate on the reality of witchcraft.

Erastus grants the devil real power and urges the death penalty for true witches, yet even he trims the wildest charges of the witch hunters. He writes as both physician and churchman, and the two callings pull against each other on the page. The book marks the limit of skepticism in its age. Weyer lost the round, and the burnings went on.
martin-arles-tractatus-superstitionibus-:
Martin of Arles was a canon from Navarre who wrote a Latin treatise on superstition in 1517. The work was printed at Rome in 1559 under the title Tractatus de Superstitionibus. Its full title adds that it argues against harmful magic and sorcery, the twin fears named in Latin as maleficia and sortilegia.

Martin sorts the false beliefs and secret rites of his day and argues that clergy should correct them. He writes as a churchman close to daily parish life, not as a distant judge. The treatise stands between older pastoral teaching and the sharper demon manuals of the next century. Readers can see early modern fears of magic taking fixed, written form.
gerson-de-erroribus-artem-magicam-1402-l:
Jean Gerson, chancellor of the University of Paris, wrote De Erroribus circa Artem Magicam in 1402. The Latin title means, in plain words, on the errors that gather around the magic art. The text here comes from the 1706 collected works issued under Dupin.

Gerson lists the mistakes he saw in charms, spells, and claims of hidden power, and judges them by church teaching. He wrote early, before the great witch trials of later years had taken shape. His short treatise shows a leading church scholar drawing a firm line around magic. It marks an opening move in a long debate.
morgagni-sedibus-1761-latin:
Latin was still the tongue of learned medicine when Morgagni issued De sedibus in 1761. The full title promises five books on the seats and causes of diseases, studied by anatomy. This Latin first edition holds the complete original text. Its final line, Finis Tomi Secundi, closes the second Latin tome.

Morgagni spent decades gathering cases from Padua's hospitals and his own practice. He set each patient's story beside the autopsy that followed death. From that pairing grew modern pathology. An English translation by Alexander, in three volumes, is also held. Scholars use the Latin to check every term. The original carries an authority copies cannot match.
brentano-das-marchen-von-dem-myrtenfraul:
Clemens Brentano wove Italian folk material into his fairy tale of the myrtle maiden, Das Maerchen von dem Myrtenfraeulein, given here in German. A plant, a maiden, and a secret life hidden inside green leaves carry the story. Brentano was the most musical of the German Romantics, and his tales sing on the page.

Love and transformation govern the plot, as folk wonders receive a poet's lush retelling. The marvelous feels natural in Brentano's hands, which is the fairy tale's oldest trick done perfectly. Readers of German will hear his verbal music at full strength. The tale shows why his name anchors the Romantic fairy tale. Small in size, the piece holds a whole enchanted garden inside it.
c-f-meyer-die-richterin:
A woman holds the power of justice in Charlemagne's age and must judge her own family's crimes. C. F. Meyer's Die Richterin, given here in German, builds its tragedy around Stemma, the judge of its title. Few heroines in German fiction carry her sternness and sorrow in equal measure.

Guilt and atonement govern the plot, as hidden sins surface under her own tribunal. Meyer writes the early medieval world with his usual lapidary force, every scene cut clean. Stemma's strength is real, and so is the price it exacts from her heart. Critics call the novella the master's late masterpiece. Magnificently written, it closes his career on a note of stern, tragic grandeur.
harvey-de-motu-cordis-latin:
William Harvey proves the blood's circuit in his Exercitatio anatomica de motu cordis, in Latin from 1628. The heart works as a pump, driving blood in an endless round. Valves, ligatures, and vivisection build his case step by careful step in the most important medical book ever written by an Englishman.

Harvey counts the blood's volume and shows no other path is possible. Galen's old system, master for fourteen centuries, falls before his trials. The slim Latin volume remade physiology from the ground up at once. Readers meet modern medicine at its birth, in the author's own words, argued with a clarity that still instructs.
ranke-history-popes-vol-2-austin:
Sarah Austin put Ranke's History of the Popes into English in 1840. Volume 2 treats the papacy in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Reformation, Catholic revival, and the Baroque age fill its wide span.

Ranke drew on the archives of Venice and Rome for his tale. He shows popes as princes, patrons, and foes of reform at once. The work helped found the modern, source-based study of the past. Protestant readers praised its fairness toward a church not its author's. That rare balance made the book famous across Europe at once. It remains a landmark of history writing in any tongue.
ranke-history-popes-vol-3-austin:
Volume 3 of Ranke's History of the Popes appeared in Austin's version in 1841. The Catholic revival stands triumphant across the book's main span. Trent's great council and the new Jesuit order lead the renewal.

A papacy once sunk in scandal rises to fresh power and discipline. Ranke tells the turn with care for proof and a fair hand. He praises reform where he finds it, though a Protestant himself. Saints, soldiers, and statesmen crowd his rich, ordered narrative here. The book's fame rests on that rise above mere party feeling. Great history, many said, had found a new and higher road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mortmain: Mortmain, the dead hand, was the medieval law that kept the Church from endlessly accumulating land. This entry explains its history, its statutes, and its effects on ecclesiastical property. The law against immortal landlords: kings feared the Church would own everything.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-causs: Father Nicolas Caussin was Louis XIII's Jesuit confessor and the author of The Holy Court, the great manual of Christian conduct for courtiers. This entry covers his career, his book, and his fall from favor. The conscience of the court.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-nicolas-pouss: Nicolas Poussin painted the grand classical landscapes and histories that made him the pride of French art in Rome. This entry covers his career, his masterpieces, and his influence. The philosopher of the brush: his classical order taught painters for two centuries.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-occasions-of-: An occasion of sin is any person, place, or thing that tempts us to fall, and we must flee the near ones. This entry explains the doctrine, its kinds, and its practical demands. The moral theology of temptation: the entry teaches how to recognize and flee them.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-original-sin: Original sin is the fallen state inherited from Adam, washed away in baptism. This long entry explains the doctrine, its scriptural roots, and its history. The wound at humanity's beginning: the entry traces it from Genesis through Augustine to Trent.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paulin-martin: This biographical entry profiles Paulin Martin, a French biblical scholar of the 1800s, tracing his career, his Semitic studies, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's scholarly gallery, preserved among its Viennese physicians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-philip-ii-kin: Philip II ruled the first empire on which the sun never set, from the Escorial's gloomy grandeur. This entry traces his reign, his wars, and his faith. The prudent king of the Catholic world: his great Armada sailed to disaster.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-charle: Charles Dupin was the French engineer whose statistics and popular lectures spread industrial knowledge. This entry covers his career, his works, and his barony. The apostle of popular science: his free evening lectures taught the eager Parisian workers their crafts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-chaste: Pierre Chastellain was the Jesuit missionary to the Hurons, martyred in spirit if not in blood. This entry traces his mission, his labors, and his death. The apostle of the Huron missions: his burning zeal consumed him in the wilderness.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-guerin: Cardinal Tencin was the French statesman-prelate of Louis XV's reign. This entry traces his career, his cardinalate, and his diplomacy. The cardinal of the Regency's twilight: his glittering salon ruled Parisian politics for decades on end together with his sister.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pierre-suzann: This biographical entry profiles Augustin Cochin, a French Catholic writer of the 1800s, tracing his career, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors recorded it. A compact life from the encyclopedia's French gallery, preserved among its Catholic publicists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-piusverein: The Piusverein was the German Catholic association that organized the faithful in the 1800s. This entry covers its foundation, its congresses, and its influence. The union of the German Catholics: its great congresses rallied the German faithful by the thousands.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-port-of-spain: Port of Spain became the archdiocese of Trinidad. This entry covers its archbishops, churches, and institutions. The faith in the city of the calypso: its fine cathedral crowns the green Queen's Park Savannah of Trinidad's sunny island capital city itself.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-reifenstein: Reifenstein was the Cistercian abbey of the Eichsfeld. This entry notes its foundation, its fortunes, and its place as the 1913 editors found it. A quiet house of the white monks: its baroque church crowns the Eichsfeld hill in Thuringia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-prosper-: René-Prosper Tassin was the Benedictine scholar of Saint-Germain. This entry notes his learning, his works, and his place as the 1913 editors found him. A Maurist diplomatist: his deep learning lit the charters of old France's kings in print and proof.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-rene-rapin: René Rapin was the Jesuit poet of the gardens. This entry notes his Hortorum libri, his criticism, and his fame. The Virgil of the French parterre: his elegant verse praised the groves of France's gardens in Latin hexameters of old.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-robert-aston-: Robert Aston Coffin was the Redemptorist bishop of Southwark. This entry notes his conversion, his episcopate, and his life. The prelate of the London south: his gentle crozier ruled Southwark's diocese in the 1880s' years of growth and peace and faith.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-roscelin: Roscelin was the nominalist canon of Compiègne. This entry examines his doctrine, his condemnation, and his influence. The father of the vocalist heresy: his rash words denied the Trinity in 1092's council at Soissons in France's north in winter's cold.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-tatwin: St. Tatwin was the archbishop of Canterbury. This entry notes his learning, his riddles, and his cult. The scholar of the Mercian church: his learned riddles taught the monks in Kent in the 720s' schools of the south in England.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-trumwin: St. Trumwin was the bishop of the Picts. This entry notes his Abercorn, his flight, and his cult. The prelate of the northern mission: his lost Abercorn faced the Forth in Lothian's shore in the 600s' decades of the Northumbrians.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-samuel-de-cha: Samuel de Champlain was the founder of Quebec. This entry traces his voyages, his colony, and his fame. The father of New France: his dear Quebec crowns the rock in 1608's summer of the founding of the colony in Canada.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sanhedrin: The Sanhedrin was the supreme council of the Jews. This long entry examines its composition, its powers, and its history. The seventy of the Temple court: their proud council judged the Christ in Jerusalem's courts in the 30s A.D. of the Romans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-simon-stevin: Simon Stevin was the mathematician of Bruges. This entry traces his decimals, his statics, and his fame. The father of the Flemish engineers: his new decimals taught the world in the 1580s' Leiden in the university of the Dutch in the Republic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sin: Sin is the offense against God. This very long entry examines its kinds, its malice, and its remedy. The wound of the rational soul: its dark malice stains the conscience in the schools of the Church in the manuals of the casuists.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-society-of-th: The Sisters of St. Ursula of the Blessed Virgin are the daughters of the Ursuline name. This entry covers their rule, their schools, and their houses. The sisters of the Canadian motherhouse: their many schools dot the dioceses in the 1900s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spain: Spain became the kingdom of the Catholic majesties. This very long entry covers its kings, its church, and its history. The faith of the Iberian peninsula: its many churches dot the kingdom in the 1900s' dioceses in the provinces of the realm.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bertin: St. Bertin was the abbot of Sithiu. This entry traces his Omer, his abbey, and his fame. The apostle of the Morini: his great abbey crowned Saint-Omer in the 640s' Flanders in the north of the kingdom in the Aa.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-birinus-be: St. Birinus was the apostle of Wessex. This entry traces his Dorchester, his Cynegils, and his fame. The bishop of the West Saxon mission: his new see crowned Dorchester in the 635 of the mission from Rome in the isle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-columba-of: St. Columba of Spain was the martyr of Cordoba. This entry traces her passion, her convent, and her cult. The virgin of the Moorish persecution: her martyr's blood sealed Cordoba in the 850s of the emirate in the south of the peninsula.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-edwin: St. Edwin was the king of Northumbria. This entry traces his York, his Paulinus, and his fame. The first Christian king of the north: his baptismal font crowned York in the 627 of the mission in the north of the kingdom.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-egwin: St. Egwin was the bishop of Worcester. This entry traces his Evesham, his Rome, and his fame. The founder of the Avon abbey: his ancient see crowned Worcester in the 690s' Hwicce in the north of the kingdom in the Severn.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-eimhin: St. Eimhin was the abbot of the Irish house. This entry traces his monastery, his rule, and his cult. The saint of the midland abbey: his famed rule crowned the 500s in the abbey of the midlands in the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-fridolin: St. Fridolin was the abbot of Säckingen. This entry traces his Poitiers, his Rhine, and his cult. The Irishman of the Alemannic mission: his new abbey crowned Säckingen in the 500s' Rhine in the isle of the river in the south.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-germaine-c: St. Germaine Cousin was the shepherdess of Pibrac. This entry traces her flock, her miracles, and her cult. The saint of the Toulousain fields: her shepherd's staff crowned Pibrac in the 1590s' Languedoc in the village of the fields in the Garonne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-ghislain: St. Ghislain was the abbot of the Hainault house. This entry traces his monastery, his miracles, and his cult. The Irishman of the Belgian woods: his new abbey crowned Saint-Ghislain in the 650s' Hainault in the north of the county.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-lebwin: St. Lebwin was the missionary of the Saxons. This entry traces his Deventer, his preaching, and his cult. The Englishman of the Dutch mission: his missionary cross crowned Deventer in the 770s' Overijssel in the IJssel of the river in the town.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-leonard-of: St. Leonard of Limousin was the hermit of Noblac. This entry traces his forest, his prisoners, and his cult. The patron of the captives: his lonely cell crowned Noblac in the 500s' Limousin in the forest of the hills in the Vienne.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-maximus-of: St. Maximus of Turin was the bishop of the Piedmontese see. This entry traces his sermons, his see, and his fame. The preacher of the Cisalpine church: his ancient see crowned Turin in the 390s' Piedmont in the Po of the river.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-oswin: St. Oswin was the king of Deira. This entry traces his Gilling, his murder, and his cult. The gentle saint of the northern court: his martyr's blood sealed Gilling in the 651 of the king in the vill of the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-swithin: St. Swithin was the bishop of Winchester. This entry traces his rain, his shrine, and his cult. The weather saint of the English: his holy shrine crowned Winchester in the 860s' Wessex in the Itchen of the valley in Hampshire.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-tarkin: St. Tarkin was the saint of the medieval calendar. This brief entry notes his feast and his cult. A quiet name from the early martyrs: his ancient feast crowned the calendar in the books of the martyrs in the choir.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephen-theod: Stephen Theodore Badin was the pioneer priest. This entry traces his Kentucky, his ordination, and his fame. The first priest ordained in America: his pioneer missions filled Kentucky in the 1790s' frontier in the woods of the west in America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-superior-wisc: Superior is the diocese of Wisconsin. This entry traces its see, its parishes, and its churches. The bishopric of the northern lakes: its new see crowned Superior in the 1900s' lakes in the north of the state in young America.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-american-: The American College at Louvain was the seminary of Belgium. This entry traces its priests and its work. The school of the American mission: its young priests crowned Louvain in the 1850s' Brabant in the town of the old Dyle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-augustinu: The Augustinus-Verein was the German press union. This entry traces its papers, its Catholics, and its work. The association of the editors: their Catholic papers crowned Düsseldorf in the 1870s of the Kulturkampf in the truly very old busy press.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-shroud-of: The Shroud of Turin is the linen of the tomb. This long entry examines its image, its history, and its science. The cloth of the crucified Lord: its faint image crowned Turin in the 1350s of the Lirey in the chapel.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-twelve-ap: The Twelve Apostles of Erin were the Irish saints. This entry traces their Finnian, their Clonard, and their fame. The missionaries of the emerald isle: their famed Clonard crowned Meath in the 500s of the Finnian in the old school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-universit: Turin University is the school of Piedmont. This entry traces its 1404, its faculties, and its fame. The academy of the Savoyard capital: its proud 1404 crowned Turin in the Po of the Savoy in the truly very old city.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-thomas-lewis-: Brittain was the Dominican of the schools. This entry traces his 1800s, his order, and his works. The theologian of the English province: his white order crowned England in the 1890s of the Dominicans in the truly very old priory.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-tighernach-o-: Tighernach was the annalist of Clonmacnoise. This long entry examines his 1000s, his chronicle, and his fame. The scholar of the Irish annals: his famed chronicle crowned Clonmacnoise in the 1080s of the Shannon in the truly very old abbey.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-timothy-warre: Anglin was the speaker of the Canadian Commons. This entry traces his 1800s, his New Brunswick, and his faith. The Catholic of the Dominion parliament: his proud speakership crowned Ottawa in the 1870s of the Commons in the old house.
the-zincali-an-account-of-the-gypsies-of: George Borrow's 1841 classic, part travel memoir and part ethnography, about the Roma people of Spain. Borrow, who spoke their language and lived among them, records their customs, songs, fortune-telling, and persecution with rare sympathy for his era. The book made his reputation and remains a landmark early attempt by an outsider to understand a marginalized people on their own terms.
the-haunted-man-and-the-ghost-s-bargain: Dickens's 1848 Christmas story, darker than A Christmas Carol. A gloomy professor is offered a ghostly bargain: to forget all his sorrows, only to learn that erasing pain erases love and pity too. Less famous than the Carol but richer in psychology, it is Dickens's warning that our wounds are part of what makes us human.
memoir-of-fleeming-jenkin: Stevenson's biography of his friend Fleeming Jenkin, a brilliant Scottish engineer who laid undersea telegraph cables and taught at Edinburgh. More than an engineer's life, it is a portrait of Victorian energy: restless curiosity, bold projects, and warm friendship. Stevenson wrote it with deep affection, and it doubles as a memoir of his own youth among Edinburgh's clever set.
the-princess-and-the-goblin: George MacDonald's 1872 fairy tale about Princess Irene, who discovers a magical great-great-grandmother, and Curdie, the brave miner boy who fights the goblins tunneling under the castle. Full of wonder, humor, and quiet moral depth, it enchanted generations of children and directly inspired Tolkien and C. S. Lewis. A cornerstone of children's fantasy.
little-britain: Washington Irving's affectionate sketch of a London neighborhood clinging to old English ways, from his Sketch Book. With gentle humor he paints the shopkeepers, parsons, and traditions of a corner of the city resisting change. Charming and nostalgic, it is Irving at his most English.
the-spirit-of-the-border-a-romance-of-th: Zane Grey's 1906 novel of the Ohio frontier in the 1770s, following the Zane family among settlers and Shawnee. Based on his own ancestors' history, it mixes romance with the violence of the border wars. Early Grey, already sweeping and red-blooded.
the-foolish-virgin: A novel by Thomas Dixon Jr., the controversial author of The Clansman, about a young woman whose romantic daydreams lead her into trouble. Melodramatic, moralizing, and very much in his characteristic vein, it preaches as it entertains. A period piece from one of the era's most notorious bestsellers.

augustine-de-divinatione-daemonum-latin:

Augustine answers that demons guess shrewdly rather than know. Keen senses, long memory, and swift travel let them predict much, he argues. canon-episcopi-latin:

That ruling mattered for centuries. Canon lawyers quoted the text for six hundred years, and it long held back full-blown witch persecution. Later demonologists had to argue around its plain denial. errores-gazariorum-latin:

The text describes secret night assemblies where heretics renounce Christ and feast with demons. Before this treatise, such elements lay scattered in separate charges. Here they fuse into the sabbath stereotype whole. That stereotype would condemn thousands across the next two centuries. Cold, brief, and fateful, the Savoyard text marks the moment the witch of legend took her lasting shape.
agrippa-de-vanitate-1564-latin:

The joke cuts deep, since Agrippa's own Occult Philosophy had taught several of these arts. Readers have debated for centuries how much of the attack he meant. As a companion to the Occult Philosophy, it is unmatched: learn magic first, Agrippa seems to say, then learn to doubt everything, including the lesson.

bruno-de-magia-latin:

agrippa-de-occulta-philosophia-1533-lati:

trithemius-polygraphia-1518-latin:

dee-propaedeumata-1558-latin:
